# linop.primme

*a compiled eigensolver for matrix-free operators*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![License: BSD 3-Clause](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-BSD_3--Clause-blue.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/BSD-3-Clause)
<!-- badges: end -->

linop.primme computes a few eigenpairs of a Hermitian operator, or a few singular triplets of a rectangular one, with the [PRIMME](https://github.com/primme/primme) library, from the operator's action alone.

The package is the compiled engine behind `method = "primme"` in [linop](https://github.com/gcol33/linop), the package for matrix-free linear operators. PRIMME (Stathopoulos and McCombs 2010; Wu, Romero and Stathopoulos 2017) restarts implicitly, so it keeps a basis of fixed small size while it iterates. Once linop.primme is installed, linop's `eigs()` and `svds()` use it by default, and the certificate that comes back with each result records which engine ran and why, so you can check what produced the numbers you report. linop.primme supports:

- **Eigenpairs of Hermitian operators.** Real and complex operators, at either end of the spectrum by value or by magnitude, and near a shift through linop's shift-invert.
- **Singular triplets of rectangular operators.** The largest or smallest singular values, with both singular vectors.
- **The same certificate as linop's own engine.** The reported values are Rayleigh quotients measured on the operator, and convergence is decided by the backward-error and residual bounds of linop's eigenpair certificate.

PRIMME 3.2.3 has its default C output streams disabled and its convergence shortcut compiled out so that linop's convergence test decides every pair. The tests check both engines against closed-form spectra, real and complex.

## Installation

The package compiles C code. Install the build tools for your operating system first:

| Operating system | Build tools |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) |
| macOS | Run `xcode-select --install` in Terminal |
| Debian / Ubuntu | Install `r-base-dev` |

Check that R can find the compiler:

```r
pkgbuild::has_build_tools(debug = TRUE)
```

Then install linop and linop.primme:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak(c("gcol33/linop", "gcol33/linop.primme"))
```

PRIMME is compiled from the copy in the package source and links against the BLAS and LAPACK libraries that R itself uses, so no separate PRIMME, BLAS or LAPACK installation is needed.

## Usage

1. Build an operator with `linop()` from linop.
2. Call `eigs()` or `svds()` from linop. The default `method = "auto"` takes PRIMME when linop.primme is installed, and `method = "primme"` asks for it by name.
3. Read which engine ran from the certificate's `dispatch` record.

A diagonal operator with three eigenvalues above the rest of its spectrum:

```{r first}
library(linop)

lam <- c(8, 7.5, 7, seq(3, 1, length.out = 997))
A <- linop_scaling(lam)
fit <- eigs(A, k = 3, method = "primme")
fit
```

The certificate records the engines considered and why PRIMME was chosen:

```{r dispatch}
certificate(fit)$dispatch$reason
```

linop.primme also exports the two calls linop makes, `primme_eigsh()` and `primme_svds()`, which take the operator as a function on a block of columns and pass PRIMME's own settings through. `primme_engine()` reports the version of the vendored PRIMME and of the calling contract with linop:

```{r engine}
linop.primme::primme_engine()
```

## Documentation

Start with [Eigenvalues and singular values](https://gillescolling.com/linop/articles/spectral.html) in linop: `eigs()` and `svds()`, the two calls that choose the engine.

- [Reading a certificate](https://gillescolling.com/linop/articles/certificates.html): what comes back attached to every result.
- `?primme_eigsh` and `?primme_svds`: the direct calls, with each PRIMME setting they pass through.
- `?primme_engine`: the version of the vendored PRIMME and of the calling contract with linop.

## Getting help

Questions and bug reports go to the [GitHub issues](https://github.com/gcol33/linop.primme/issues). A bug report is easiest to act on with a small reproducible example, for instance made with [reprex](https://reprex.tidyverse.org/).

## Acknowledgements

The eigensolver is [PRIMME](https://github.com/primme/primme) by Andreas Stathopoulos, Eloy Romero, Lingfei Wu and co-authors at the College of William & Mary (Stathopoulos and McCombs 2010, [doi:10.1145/1731022.1731031](https://doi.org/10.1145/1731022.1731031); Wu, Romero and Stathopoulos 2017, [doi:10.1137/16M1082214](https://doi.org/10.1137/16M1082214)). Every eigenpair and singular triplet this package returns is computed by it.
